summary: Defines a new name form for the otherName field of an X.509 Subject Alternative Name, tying a certificate to the service name and domain name used by a DNS SRV record. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: A certificate can say not just which website it belongs to but which service at that website it is for.

how to put a service name in a certificate
how do name constraints work for srvname
subtitle: A certificate name that says which service at a domain a server is allowed to provide.

tldr.problem: When a client finds a server through a DNS SRV lookup, it may need to check that the server is authorized for that service, not just that it has a given host name. The usual dNSName form only holds a host name in preferred name syntax.
tldr.mechanism: The SRVName is a new otherName form for the Subject Alternative Name extension. It holds a service name and domain name in the form _Service.Name, matching the parts of a DNS SRV record.
tldr.outcome: A relying party can tie a certificate to a service within a domain. The text defines matching rules and name constraints for it.

today: RFC 4985 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 2782 and RFC 3280.

sections.title: Why Certificates Need a Service Name
sections.content:
RFC 4985 specifies a name form for X.509 certificates. A relying party can use it to verify that a particular host is authorized to provide a specific service within a domain.

RFC 2782 defines the DNS SRV resource record, which lets clients ask for a specific service for a domain and get back the names of available servers. Existing certificate name forms support authentication of a host name, which helps when the client already knows the host name. When the name is discovered through an SRV lookup, the client may also need to authenticate the server's authorization for the requested service.

DNS may supply trusted information, but in many cases the binding between host and service needs extra credentials. The current dNSName form allows only host names in the preferred name syntax of RFC 1034, so it cannot express a service related to a domain.
sections.plainLanguage: Knowing a computer's name is not enough. You also want proof that this computer is allowed to run the service you asked for.

sections.title: The SRVName Form
sections.content:
The SRVName is an otherName inside the GeneralName structure of SubjectAltName, defined in RFC 3280. It is identified by id-on-dnsSRV, which is { id-on 7 }, and its type is an IA5String of at least one character.

It MUST contain a service name and a domain name in the form _Service.Name, consistent with those components of an SRV record in RFC 2782. Service is the symbolic name of the service, from Assigned Numbers or defined locally, with an underscore prepended to avoid collisions with ordinary DNS labels. If Assigned Numbers names the service, that is the only name allowed. The service is case insensitive. Name is the DNS domain name where the service is located.

The protocol part of an SRV record (_Service._Proto.Name) is left out. This lets one certificate with a single SRVName cover a host offering several protocols, and it keeps name constraint rules simpler. The SRVName does not verify the protocol in use.

A present SRVName MUST NOT be used to identify a host unless the security protocol in use specifies this name form and the service has a defined service name under RFC 2782, or local policy configures its use. The document sets no new conditions for using SRV records for discovery.
sections.plainLanguage: The name is a label like _mail.example.com: the kind of service, then the place. It leaves out which delivery method is used.

sections.title: Internationalized Domain Names
sections.content:
IA5String holds only ASCII, so implementations MUST convert an internationalized domain name to ASCII Compatible Encoding as described in section 4 of RFC 3490 before storing it in the Name part. The RFC adds clarifications: the name is a stored string, so AllowUnassigned is not set; UseSTD3ASCIIRules is set; each label is processed with ToASCII; and label separators change to U+002E.

Comparing DNS names for equality MUST be a case-insensitive exact match on the whole domain name. For name constraints it is a case-insensitive exact match label by label. Implementations SHOULD convert IDNs back to Unicode for display, using ToUnicode and skipping the last step. They MUST allow for extra space, because an ACE label begins with xn-- and can need as many as five ASCII characters for one international character.
sections.plainLanguage: Names with accented or non-Latin letters are turned into plain letters for storing, and turned back for people to read.

sections.title: Name Constraint Matching
sections.content:
A CA can limit SRVNames with the name constraints extension of RFC 3280, using a restriction in SRVName form. A restriction can be a full SRVName (_mail.example.com), just a service name (_mail), or just a DNS name (example.com). The service part and the DNS part are handled separately.

If the restriction includes a service name, only an SRVName with that service name satisfies it. If it has none, any SRVName matching the domain part satisfies it. A DNS name restriction is satisfied by any name made by adding subdomains on the left, so www.host.example.com satisfies host.example.com but 1host.example.com does not.
sections.plainLanguage: A certificate authority can say, you may only use this for mail, or only inside this domain, and the rules check each part.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The assignment of services to hosts can change. Implementers should revoke old certificates that no longer reflect the current assignment, so that issued certificates stay up to date.

When the name form is used to strengthen authentication of discovery through an SRV query, all security considerations of RFC 2782 apply.
sections.plainLanguage: If a computer stops running a service, its old certificate should be cancelled so nobody trusts it for that job.
